The FY2017 defense authorization gathered dozens of scattered Defense Department authorities for training, equipping, and advising foreign forces into a single chapter of Title 10, with common definitions, oversight, and evaluation rules.

## Key provisions

- 10 U.S.C. 333: the global train-and-equip authority, successor to the Section 1206 program, requiring State Department concurrence.
- 10 U.S.C. 332: institutional capacity building for foreign defense ministries.
- 10 U.S.C. 383: assessment, monitoring, and evaluation of security cooperation programs.
- 10 U.S.C. 362: the Defense Department Leahy law.
- Made the Defense Security Cooperation Agency responsible for the consolidated budget and workforce.

## Why it matters

It marks the growth of the Defense Department's own assistance programs alongside State's traditional role under the [Foreign Assistance Act](faa-1961.qmd) and the [Arms Export Control Act](aeca-1976.qmd). The division of labor between Title 10 and Title 22 assistance is one of the central questions in security assistance policy.

## Current status

In force and adjusted in most later defense authorizations.
